subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on writing hypotheses and identifying variables, then mark my answer against the OCR spec.
promptWeak: Explain the difference between an independent and dependent variable for GCSE OCR Psychology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: A hypothesis that predicts there will be no difference or relationship is called the:
questions.explain: The null hypothesis predicts no difference or no relationship; the alternative hypothesis predicts a difference or correlation.

questions.q: 'Students who revise with flashcards will score higher than those who do not.' This is best described as:
options: An alternative hypothesis predicting a difference
questions.explain: It predicts a difference between two conditions, so it is an alternative hypothesis (a directional one, as it states the direction).

questions.q: In an experiment, the variable the researcher deliberately manipulates is the:
questions.explain: The independent variable (IV) is the one the researcher changes; the dependent variable (DV) is what is measured.

questions.q: A study tests whether noise affects test scores. What is the dependent variable?
questions.explain: The DV is what is measured, here the test score; the level of noise is the manipulated IV.

questions.q: A variable other than the IV that could affect the DV if not controlled is an:
questions.explain: Extraneous variables are unwanted variables that could influence the DV; they are controlled, e.g. through standardisation.

questions.q: In which experimental design does the SAME group of participants take part in both conditions?
questions.explain: In repeated measures the same participants do all conditions; in independent measures different participants do each condition.

questions.q: A researcher uses different participants in the 'quiet' and 'noisy' conditions so no one is tested twice. This design is:
questions.explain: Different participants in each condition is an independent measures design.

questions.q: Which of these is a sampling method listed in the OCR spec?
questions.explain: The OCR GCSE spec lists random, opportunity and self-selected sampling (stratified and systematic are not required at this level).

questions.q: A researcher puts up a poster asking for volunteers to take part. Which sampling method is this?
questions.explain: When participants volunteer in response to an advert, it is self-selected (volunteer) sampling.

questions.q: Which organisation's Code of Ethics and Conduct guides psychological research in the OCR spec?
questions.explain: Research is guided by the British Psychological Society's (BPS) Code of Ethics and Conduct.

questions.q: After a study, a researcher explains its true aims and checks participants are not distressed. This is:
questions.explain: Debriefing is telling participants the full aims afterwards and checking their wellbeing; it can help deal with prior deception.

questions.q: An experiment carried out in a highly controlled setting is a:
questions.explain: A laboratory experiment is conducted in a controlled setting; field experiments occur in natural surroundings, and natural experiments use naturally-occurring IVs.

questions.q: Researchers study behaviour on a real train platform, manipulating whether a confederate wears a uniform. This is a:
questions.explain: Manipulating an IV in a real-world setting is a field experiment, which tends to have higher ecological validity.

questions.q: A questionnaire item that gives fixed response options for participants to choose from uses:
questions.explain: Closed questions offer fixed choices (easy to analyse); open questions allow free responses (richer qualitative data).

questions.q: An interview that follows a fixed set of questions in the same order for every participant is:
questions.explain: A structured interview uses the same fixed questions for all, making it more reliable and easier to compare.

questions.q: An observation where participants do NOT know they are being watched is described as:
questions.explain: A covert observation is hidden from participants (reducing demand characteristics); an overt observation is open and known.

questions.q: As hours of sleep go up, reported tiredness goes down. This pattern is a:
questions.explain: When one co-variable rises as the other falls, it is a negative correlation.

questions.q: Data collected first-hand by the researcher for their own study is called:
questions.explain: Primary data is collected first-hand by the researcher; secondary data comes from existing sources such as other studies.

questions.q: For the data set 3, 5, 5, 7, 20, which statement is correct?
questions.explain: Ordered: 3,5,5,7,20. The median (middle value) is 5. The mode is 5, the range is 17, and the mean is 8.

questions.q: Which graph is most appropriate for displaying the relationship between two co-variables in a correlation?
questions.explain: A scatter diagram (scattergram) plots two co-variables to show the strength and direction of a correlation.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Psychology (J203) specification; Research Methods
